response.task_summary: Predict an ANES respondent’s political preference/party-related outcome from attitudes, issue positions, and demographics, prioritizing stable ideological signals over domain-specific artifacts.

ranking.rationale: Direct self-reported party identification is usually the strongest stable predictor of political outcomes.
General ideological self-placement is highly predictive and tends to transfer across election years.
Warmth toward Democrats captures durable partisan affect.
Warmth toward Republicans captures durable partisan affect and complements the Democratic thermometer.
Direct affect toward the Democratic Party is a strong, semantically stable partisan signal.
Direct affect toward the Republican Party is a strong, semantically stable partisan signal.
Party identification is a core political identity feature with broad predictive value.
Which party best represents views is a direct partisan alignment indicator.
Perceived party representation of views is closely tied to partisan preference.
Belief that parties represent views reasonably well reflects partisan engagement and alignment.
Preference for unified versus divided government is a stable institutional preference linked to partisanship.
Views on which party favors stronger government are ideological and relatively durable.
Views on military spending cut are policy-based and informative about ideology.
Abortion attitudes are a classic stable issue-position predictor of political preference.
Gun control importance is a durable issue attitude with strong partisan association.
Religiosity is a stable social value correlated with political orientation.
Attitudes toward protests reflect broader civic and ideological orientation.
Views on government waste are a stable small-government versus big-government signal.
Beliefs about voting as the only way to have a say indicate civic orientation and engagement.
Belief that voting matters is a general political efficacy signal.
Norms about voting even when uninterested capture civic duty and engagement.
Norms about voting when one’s party cannot win reflect political participation orientation.
Interest in elections is a stable engagement measure that supports prediction.
Membership in political organizations indicates durable political involvement.
Trying to influence others during campaigns reflects active political participation.
Attending rallies is a strong engagement indicator, though somewhat behaviorally noisy.
Displaying campaign materials signals partisan activism and engagement.
Donating to campaigns is a strong but more selective participation signal.
Registration status is predictive of political participation, though partly outcome-adjacent.
Media trust can correlate with political orientation and information environment.
Watching campaign TV content reflects political interest and exposure.
Radio campaign exposure is a weaker but still relevant engagement signal.
Magazine campaign exposure indicates political information seeking.
Internet campaign exposure is informative but can be more platform- and era-dependent.
General evaluation of national conditions is predictive but more time-sensitive than core ideology.
Assessment of government economic policy is relevant but can vary with current events.
Perceived economic change is useful but somewhat cyclical and domain-dependent.
Perceived national strength is informative but more contingent on the election context.
Most important national problem captures issue salience, though it is noisy and time-specific.
Guaranteed jobs and income reflects economic ideology, but wording can be survey-specific.
Government services and spending is a classic policy preference, though less direct than ideology.
Defense spending preference is policy-relevant but often less central to the target.
Presidential thermometer is predictive but can be more election- and incumbent-specific.
Vice-presidential thermometer is similar to the president thermometer but usually weaker.
Issue-specific party preference on environment is useful but narrower and more context-dependent.
Issue-specific party preference on inflation is informative but highly election-era dependent.
Issue-specific party preference on unemployment is relevant but narrower than core ideology.
State can encode geography and regional politics, but it is a brittle domain identifier for OOD generalization.
Race/ethnicity is predictive through demographic patterns, but it risks shortcut learning and fairness concerns.
Education is a demographic proxy that can help but may encourage shortcut reliance.
Age is moderately predictive but often acts as a demographic shortcut rather than a stable causal signal.
Gender is a demographic shortcut with limited semantic stability across domains.
Occupation group is noisy and can reflect sampling or socioeconomic artifacts more than robust preference.
Election year is a strong domain identifier and should be heavily downweighted for OOD generalization.
